title: Is it just me or is the mantra…
author: 00G_WAY
selftext: Work on a branch in an isolated worktree. No subagents. Commit and push as you go. Merge at the end and cleanup.

comments.author: Best_Season_2674
comments.body: Full automation in game dev makes the process way longer and costly. The rabbit holes and circles I’ve seen it do without proper direction and redirection is absurd

replies.author: FreeQ1337
replies.body: Yes i noticed best progress (albeit slower) is to babysit it if you have the time.

replies.author: Best_Season_2674
replies.body: I agree. It gets the best results, it’s not the greatest at knowing and implementing the proper procedures to get the best performance and quality on its own. It often takes short cuts and mixes irrational systems and I’ve caught it doing some ridiculous things even with my explicit direction, proper graph file set up, parameters project wide. It’s insanely smart and great at coding game mechanics. That’s about it haha

replies.author: FreeQ1337
replies.body: Yeah, its like a teenager injected with coding skills. It can do the thing you need it to, but god it needs a guidance to not make up bullshit.

replies.author: 00G_WAY
replies.body: for real. it’s so much better to treat these agents like individuals accomplishing specific tasks that need iteration.

comments.author: spartagon123
comments.body:
No sub agents? 

Claude has gotten very good and efficient at using sub agents. You might get better token efficiency using some...

replies.author: Best_Season_2674
replies.body: Def yes a coordinating agent with sub agent delegation. Over all only personally working directly with the coordinator

replies.author: 00G_WAY
replies.body: Token efficiency is never the problem for me. I care only about quality work. Sub agents are great for longform tasks that you want your agent to babysit for you. But if you really just want weaker models doing more work, then you can spawn those agents yourself and then actually talk to them instead of waiting on sub agents that you have to send messages to your initial agent to even access.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body: Sub agents can in some cases improve work quality. If a sub agents is given a sub task, it can focus more soley on that one task or part of the instructions without it's context being crowded by other things.

replies.author: 00G_WAY
replies.body: and if I do allow subagents, I allow one or two maximum. likely sonnet. but the fact of the matter is: if I know that I want my opus agent to spawn sonnet agents to divide work, I have to be really careful because it will give the sonnet agent stuff to do and just wait around for the sonnet agent to finish. if I wanted sonnet to do my work, I would just use a sonnet model instead of opus (or fable). The beauty of making sure that your model doesn’t spawn any sub agents is that you get the model you requested to do the work you’re asking for.

replies.author: UncleJoesLandscaping
replies.body: What exactly do you use sub agents for? I have found coming up with what I want to be the bottle neck. As long as I can describe it Opus 5.5 has been able to code it pretty much every time.

replies.author: spartagon123
replies.body:
It depends on the kind of work your doing. If it's more exploratory and trying things out, then yeah, you are often the bottleneck. But if it's a whole product that you already have a huge vision already in mind for then you might be waiting more for Claude. 


Claude is already smart enough to use sub agents decently. For example it might spawn a sub agents to do code exploration. Say you ask it to change feature x. It might spawn one agent to find where in the code feature x is and what files need to change. This is because it might do a lot of searches that actually pull up the wrong files as it looks around. Those wrong files and searches are extra tokens. Once it found what it needs, it passes that to a new agent only the ones it needs to do the work. That way the coding agent doesn't have extra context that's not relevant and operates more efficiently. 

Another example is running tests. Tests often produce tons of logs and data. You can wrap it in an agent that reads the output and only passes back failures or whats relevant, rather than bloating the context of the main session with test logs.
